title: 2 Samuel 4:9–12
context: David answers Rechab and Baanah with an oath by the LORD who has redeemed his soul out of all adversity. He reminds them that he executed the man who brought news of Saul’s death in Ziklag, thinking it good news, and declares that wicked men who kill a righteous person in his own house on his bed deserve even greater judgment. At David’s command, his young men kill them, cut off their hands and feet, and hang them beside the pool in Hebron. Ishbosheth’s head is buried in Abner’s grave in Hebron. Both traditions read the passage as David refusing to gain the throne through murder, entrusting his deliverance to the LORD, and acting to punish bloodshed done in his name.

verses.text: David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said to them, “As the LORD lives, who has redeemed my soul out of all adversity,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that David begins with an oath by the LORD who has redeemed his soul out of all adversity. By recalling God’s past deliverance, David shows that he does not need murderers to secure his throne; he trusts the LORD who has protected him throughout his trials.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that David’s oath frames his whole response in terms of God’s faithfulness to him. Both traditions agree that David’s confidence rests on the LORD, not on the actions of those who claim to serve his cause, and that this confidence shapes his rejection of the killers.

verses.text: when someone told me, ‘Behold, Saul is dead,’ thinking that he brought good news, I seized him and killed him in Ziklag, which was the reward I gave him for his news.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that David reminds them of the man who reported Saul’s death expecting reward, whom David had executed in Ziklag (2 Samuel 1:1–16). The comparison shows David’s consistency: he will not reward those who bring him power through the death of the LORD’s anointed or of Saul’s house.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that David’s earlier action set a precedent, establishing that his throne would not be built on the deaths of his rivals. Both traditions agree that David’s consistency here underscores his integrity and his refusal to profit from bloodshed.

verses.text: How much more, when wicked men have slain a righteous person in his own house on his bed, should I not now require his blood from your hand, and rid the earth of you?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that David calls Ishbosheth a righteous person killed in his own house on his bed. Whatever Ishbosheth’s weaknesses, he was innocent of any crime deserving death, and David regards his murder as wicked, deserving judgment that would rid the land of the killers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that David’s judgment expresses the principle that shed blood demands accountability (Genesis 9:6). Both traditions agree that David acts as a king upholding justice, refusing to let murder go unpunished even when its victim was his rival.

verses.text: David commanded his young men, and they killed them, cut off their hands and their feet, and hanged them up beside the pool in Hebron. But they took the head of Ishbosheth and buried it in Abner’s grave in Hebron.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers point out that David has the killers executed and their hands and feet cut off, and their bodies hung by the pool in Hebron as a public warning. The severity reflects the gravity of the crime in its setting, and the narrator records it soberly without dwelling on it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the public nature of the punishment and the burial of Ishbosheth’s head in Abner’s grave. Both traditions agree that the passage shows David honoring the dead of Saul’s house and punishing their murderers, and that God’s purpose for David is advancing through, yet not because of, the violence of others.
